card.title: iPhone 16 Pro no power/no charge traced to shorted CP3200B1 IC

source.title: I Think I Found the iPhone 16 Pro's Next Common Failure (And How To Fix It) — VCC Board Repairs - Jesse Cruz

claims.statement: An immediate high current draw (2.4A-2.5A) at 4.2V DC input prior to pressing the power button indicates a short circuit on a main power rail (VDD Main).
claims.evidence: Plugging the custom DC battery cable into the shorted iPhone 16 Pro board immediately pulled 2.4A-2.5A at 4.2V without prompting to boot.
claims.quote: Look at that. We actually have a huge current draw... 2.4 amp draw, 2.5 before prompt to boot. Meaning, I'm only connecting the battery to it and it's pulling current. That tells me there's a short on a main power rail.

claims.statement: The CP3200B1 charging IC on iPhone 16 series boards can short to ground on VDD Main, causing total board failure and zero charging response.
claims.evidence: Thermal imaging identified CP3200B1 heating up under 4.2V DC input; removing CP3200B1 instantly cleared the 2.5A short on VDD Main.
claims.quote: It is the CP3200B1G0... CP3200B1 for the 16 series. So, basically all the 16 models will use this charging IC... our fault was no power caused by a main short that happens to be on the charging IC.

claims.statement: Mechanic USB-C tester outer pin readings present as a 0.07 short value on a faulted charging/main circuit board versus OL on a known-good board.
claims.evidence: The customer board registered 0.07 on the outer pins of the Mechanic USB-C reader, whereas the working donor board showed OL.
claims.quote: If you notice, the readings are no longer 0.07, they're now OL. So, that's what known good readings should actually be... 0.07 is basically a short on the mechanic reader, and on the known good, it actually shows OL.

procedure: Test charging port connector using a USB-C circuit tester to verify outer pin diode/short readings against a known-good donor board.
Connect 4.2V DC power supply to the battery connector using a custom battery boot cable to monitor initial current draw before pressing power button.
Carefully trim and pry the shield bracket near the charging controller section using wire cutters to expose the ICs.
Apply 4.2V current to the board and inspect under a macro thermal camera to pinpoint the component generating localized heat.
Apply Amtech flux and remove shorted IC CP3200B1 with hot air at 380°C and 50% air flow.
Prep pads with 183°C Kester 63/37 leaded solder and wick pads flat using hot air.
If adjacent solder mask was scraped or traces exposed, apply UV solder mask and cure with UV light and gentle heat.
Align new CP3200B1 IC to orientation mark and solder into place with hot air.
If secondary IC SN2012027 was mechanically damaged during shield removal, replace it with new SN2012027 IC.
Place board on steel block with cooling fan, then re-test DC power supply prompt-to-boot sequence and USB-C charging function.

measurements.context: Current draw at 4.2V before prompt to boot on shorted VDD Main

measurements.point: Mechanic USB-C tester outer pins (shorted board)
measurements.context: Short reading on faulted board charging port pins

measurements.point: Mechanic USB-C tester outer pins (known-good board)
measurements.context: Normal open loop reading on working board

tools: Seek Compact Pro thermal camera with macro lens
cautions: SOURCE RISK: Prying off board shields with wire cutters can chip or crush adjacent micro ICs (e.g., SN2012027 charging controller).
Mark orientation dot before IC removal to ensure correct orientation during replacement.
Avoid excessive hot air duration on sandwich boards to prevent interposer solder separation.
card.caveats: A VDD Main short can be caused by many different capacitors or ICs across the iPhone board; CP3200B1 is one specific failure location.
